quality_reasons.text: Nurse was warm, patient and reassuring, built good rapport, and correctly explained referred shoulder pain
Serious clinical safety misses: acetaminophen from three sources not caught, the 101.8 fever with incision redness not addressed, and a tub bath recommended against discharge instructions
Appropriately conferenced the on-call surgical PA for the drain question

flags.text: Acetaminophen overdose risk not caught: patient takes hydrocodone/acetaminophen (Norco), plus Extra Strength Tylenol two every six hours, plus NyQuil at night; the nurse said Tylenol is fine instead of warning about the combined acetaminophen total
flags.evidence: Oh, yeah, I'm also taking regular Tylenol. The Extra Strength. Two every six hours, like the bottle says.
paraphrases: The nurse failed to recognise that the patient is taking acetaminophen from several sources (Norco, Extra Strength Tylenol and NyQuil), exceeding the safe daily maximum.
Patient's combined Tylenol intake likely exceeds 4 g/day, with liver toxicity risk, but the nurse reassured her it was fine.
Clinical safety: duplicate acetaminophen products (hydrocodone-APAP plus OTC Tylenol plus nighttime cold medicine) not identified.
negatives: Nurse told the patient no alcohol while on hydrocodone.
Patient takes Extra Strength Tylenol as directed on the bottle.

flags.text: Fever not properly assessed: the husband corrected the temperature to 101.8 last night (with a red, warm ring around the umbilical incision), but the nurse treated it as a low-grade 100.8, never addressed 101.8 (above her own call-back threshold of 101) and relayed 100.8 to the PA
flags.evidence: no, Immy, last night it was a hundred and one point eight, I wrote it down
paraphrases: The husband reported a temperature of 101.8 F, which the nurse ignored, calling it a low-grade fever and not escalating possible infection.
Possible post-operative wound infection (fever plus warm redness at the belly-button incision) dismissed as normal healing.
Nurse missed the corrected temperature reading of 101.8 and told the PA she was only low-grade, so the fever was never escalated.
negatives: Nurse explained the shoulder pain was referred gas pain.
Low-grade temperature after surgery is common.

flags.text: Nurse recommended a warm tub bath for back soreness, contradicting the discharge instructions she had read earlier (no tub baths, hot tubs or swimming for two weeks) while the patient has fresh incisions and a drain
flags.evidence: a nice warm bath would help with the soreness
paraphrases: The nurse told the patient to soak in the tub, although the discharge instructions prohibit baths for two weeks.
Incorrect advice: tub bath suggested three days after surgery with a JP drain in place.
Misinformation: bath recommended contrary to post-op wound-care instructions.
negatives: Nurse confirmed showers are allowed after 48 hours.

decoys.text: Nurse dismissed the patient's right shoulder pain
decoys.why_not: Right shoulder pain after laparoscopy is classic referred pain from the CO2 gas; the nurse explained it correctly and gave red-flag advice (sudden worsening, shortness of breath, chest pain -> 911).
decoys.evidence: That's the gas they use to inflate your belly.
paraphrases: The patient's right shoulder pain was attributed to gas without a proper assessment.
Nurse brushed off new shoulder pain as referred pain from surgery.

decoys.text: Nurse discussed the patient's medical details with her husband, a third party
decoys.why_not: The verified patient explicitly said on the call that Rob can be told anything; the nurse documented her consent.
decoys.evidence: So you can talk to him about anything, whatever you need, he knows more than me right now.
paraphrases: Patient health information was shared with the husband on speakerphone without written authorization.
Privacy: the nurse discussed medications and symptoms with the spouse.

decoys.text: Nurse did not answer the drain question herself and deferred it to the surgical PA
decoys.why_not: Drain management belongs to the surgical team; conferencing the on-call PA, who answered with the removal protocol, was the correct escalation.
decoys.evidence: So that one I'm actually going to hand over to the surgical team
paraphrases: The nurse deflected the drain question to the on-call physician assistant instead of answering it.
Drain question was handed off to the surgical team, delaying an answer.

acceptable_flags.text: Phone menu option 3 routes refill calls to billing; patient needed three tries
Controlled pain medication refill needs the surgeon; patient running low
Constipation since surgery / opioid side effects
NyQuil plus hydrocodone sedation / drowsiness interaction
Long hold to reach the PA / headset cutting out
